questions.explain: Sharding distributes different rows to different servers by shard key, so writes go to different machines. Replication keeps the full dataset on every node (no write scaling), and partitioning is a storage optimization within one logical database.
options: Replication, because every replica holds the full dataset and absorbs writes
Partitioning, because partition-aligned indexes let writes go to separate servers
Sharding, because it is the only pattern that scales write throughput horizontally across servers
Indexed views, because they pre-compute writes for faster commits
questions.q: A 500GB table suffers slow full scans, a reporting workload is overwhelming the primary, and a write-heavy app has outgrown a single server's I/O capacity. Which architectural tool matches the write-heavy problem?

questions.explain: CDC marks deletes as 1, inserts as 2, before-update images as 3, and after-update images as 4. Updates appear as a before/after pair.
options: An insert of a new row
The before-update image of an updated row
A delete of a row
The after-update image of an updated row
questions.q: In SQL Server Change Data Capture, what does __$operation = 3 represent in a change table row?

questions.explain: SqlClient pooling is keyed by the exact connection string, so per-pod configuration drift silently fragments one logical pool into many small ones. Connection strings should be built once, centrally.
options: The server's CPU count — pools scale with available cores
The application's process ID — each process always gets one shared pool
The Windows user account — each login gets a private pool
The exact connection string — even a whitespace difference creates a separate pool
questions.q: According to the chapter, what determines which logical pool a SqlClient connection belongs to, and why does it matter?

questions.explain: Beyond about 2 x cores + disks, connections queue behind each other and throughput actually drops due to lock contention and context switching. Queuing in the pool is far cheaper than hundreds of workers fighting over schedulers.
options: Approximately 2 x num_cores + num_disks; beyond that, throughput decreases from lock contention and context switching
Exactly 100 connections per CPU core regardless of storage
As many as the OS allows, because queuing in the pool wastes latency
One connection per application thread, since SqlClient pools eliminate contention
questions.q: What is the chapter's rule of thumb for the optimal number of active database connections?

questions.explain: Because readable secondaries lag the primary, reads requiring the latest data must go to the primary — route reads there briefly after a write or accept that certain reads are always primary-bound.
options: Disable synchronous commit so the secondary always matches the primary instantly
Route reads to the primary for a brief window after any write, or keep freshness-critical reads primary-bound
Increase Max Pool Size so pooled connections always land on the primary
Enable forced parameterization so both reads use the same cached plan
questions.q: A user creates an order and immediately reads their order history, but the read goes to a lagging readable secondary and the order is missing. What is the chapter's recommended fix for this read-after-write problem?
